own_scenes.desc: Tras Roxanne Shanté, las mujeres se impusieron a sus colegas. MC Lyte, de Brooklyn, a los dieciséis años abordó el crack a través de una relación en «I Cram to Understand U (Sam)»; Lyte as a Rock (1988), primera rapera nominada al Grammy y de las primeras en hacer un diss record. Cheryl James y Sandra Denton, compañeras de enfermería que trabajaban en Sears, se unieron al productor Hurby «Luv Bug» Azor: Salt-N-Pepa (con DJ Spinderella desde 1987) contestaban a los hombres siendo ellas mismas y fueron las primeras raperas en llegar al platino. Dana Owens, del instituto de Irvington, llamó a su grupo Ladies Fresh y a sí misma Queen Latifah; Mark the 45 King le produjo la maqueta que llegó a Monica Lynch en Tommy Boy, y All Hail the Queen (1989) la hizo la gran voz feminista del hip hop.

refs.q: I just loved the spirit of Salt-N-Pepa and the fact that they were really some of the first women in hip-hop to answer back to the guys.
refs.para: Janette Beckman (documentary photographer): I just loved the spirit of Salt-N-Pepa and the fact that they were really some of the first women in hip-hop to answer back to the guys.

refs.q: She had that going on, too.
refs.para: There weren’t a lot of female MCs out there at that point. Of course, Salt-N-Pepa sort of wrote their own book as far as it’s R&B, it’s hip-hop, sexy type of thing. But save for Lyte, there weren’t too many in the female hip-hop category that was taking it from this sort of hard, cool, “I can hang with the guys and get respect from the guys, and you can put me up with any of them.” She had that going on, too.
